item.title: Al-Kindi (801–873): Islamic Neoplatonism and the Philosophical Foundations of Magic
item.description:
Life and Philosophical Mission

Al-Kindi (801–873), Arab philosopher and theologian, was the first major Islamic philosopher and one of the greatest intellectual figures of the Islamic golden age. Born in Kufa, educated in Baghdad, Al-Kindi served the Abbasid caliphs as a court philosopher before being persecuted by orthodox theologians.

Al-Kindi’s mission was to synthesize Greek philosophy (especially Neoplatonism and Aristotelian logic) with Islamic theology. Though he wrote on mathematics, astronomy, medicine, and epistemology, his central preoccupation was reconciling reason and revelation, philosophy and theology.

item.title: Giordano Bruno (1548–1600)
item.description:
What Bruno Called His Work: Magic and Infinite Philosophy

Giordano Bruno (1548–1600), an Italian Dominican friar turned itinerant philosopher, explicitly embraced the term magia—magic—for his philosophical project. Unlike Ficino’s careful avoidance of the term and Agrippa’s explanation that occult philosophy was natural philosophy, Bruno unambiguously positioned his work as magical. He called himself a magus and his philosophy magia naturalis operating through hermetic correspondences.

Yet for Bruno, this magic was not transgressive superstition but the highest form of natural philosophy: the knowledge and practice of infinite being, the cosmological correspondences binding all things in an infinite universe, the divine unity underlying apparent multiplicity. Bruno’s magia was grounded in the recovery of Egyptian wisdom (sapienza egizia), preserved in the Hermetic corpus and in magical traditions descended from antiquity.

item.title: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494)
item.description:
What Pico Called His Work: Universal Theology

Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), an Italian nobleman and philosopher born in Mirandola, articulated his intellectual project as the creation of a philosophia universalis—a universal philosophy reconciling all the world’s wisdom traditions into a unified system revealing divine truth. His project was explicitly theological: he aimed to show that Platonism, Aristotelianism, Judaism, Christianity, and Islam all contained fragments of a single perennial wisdom, and that by synthesizing these traditions, Renaissance Christian philosophy could recover the complete truth about God, creation, and human nature.

item.title: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535)
item.description:
What Agrippa Called His Work: Occult Philosophy

Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a German polymath trained in theology, law, medicine, and philosophy, explicitly called his work philosophia occultalis—occult philosophy. Unlike Ficino’s careful emphasis on philosophia naturalis and prisca theologia, or Pico’s philosophia universalis, Agrippa embraced the term “occult” (occultus = hidden), positioning his project as the investigation of hidden correspondences, secret properties, and concealed operations woven through creation.

Yet “occult” for Agrippa did not mean transgressive or demonic. It meant hidden according to natural law—accessible to the trained investigator who understood mathematics, astrology, and the correspondences binding together all levels of being. Agrippa’s Three Books of Occult Philosophy (De Occulta Philosophia, 1531) presents a comprehensive system of magia naturalis (natural magic) and magia caeremonialis (ceremonial magic) grounded in the belief that all phenomena—celestial, terrestrial, human—operate according to proportions, correspondences, and hidden connections accessible to knowledge and manipulation.

item.title: Iamblichus (245–325): Theurgy, Divine Ritual, and the Operative Neoplatonism
item.description:
Life and Theurgical Revolution

Iamblichus (245–325), Syrian Neoplatonic philosopher and mystic, radically transformed Neoplatonic philosophy by developing theurgy—divine-working ritual—as central to spiritual practice. Born in Chalcis, Iamblichus studied under Porphyry but moved beyond his teacher’s skepticism toward theurgy, creating a philosophy in which ritual operation became crucial for the soul’s ascent toward the divine.

Iamblichus founded a school in Apamea that became the center of theurgical Neoplatonism. Though no complete writings survive, his teachings shaped subsequent Neoplatonism through his students and through reports by later philosophers. His reputation as a wonder-worker and his insistence that theurgy permitted direct communion with the gods made him a towering figure in pagan philosophy’s final centuries.

item.title: John Dee (1527–1609)
item.description:
What Dee Called His Work: The Mathematics of Nature

John Dee (1527–1609), an English mathematician, astrologer, and natural philosopher born in London, explicitly positioned his intellectual work within the framework of mathematica—the science of quantity, proportion, and geometric truth. His foundational text, the Monas Hieroglyphica (1564), bears the subtitle Libellus Sapientiae, and throughout his writings Dee describes himself as recovering ancient mathematical wisdom (prisca sapientia mathematica) encoded in the sacred geometry of creation itself. He called his work philosophia naturalis—natural philosophy—understood as the systematic investigation of nature through mathematical principles.

item.title: Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499)
item.description:
What Ficino Called His Work: Actor Terminology

Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), an Italian Catholic priest and philosopher born in Figline Valdarno, explicitly rejected the label “magic” for his intellectual and medical projects. His own terminology was precise and defensive: he called his work philosophia naturalis (natural philosophy), medicina (medicine), and prisca theologia (ancient theology). These self-descriptions positioned his work squarely within legitimate Renaissance intellectual frameworks, not as transgressive magical practice.

In letters to patrons and in the prefatory material to his Platonic translations, Ficino frames himself as a natural philosopher engaged in understanding how the cosmos operates according to rational principles. His De Vita (1489), his most ambitious work on the relationship between celestial influences and human health, is presented explicitly as a medical treatise. The work addresses his patron Lorenzo de’ Medici with the claim that Ficino is teaching the art of health preservation (ars conservationis vitae) through understanding natural causes. The planetary correspondences he describes, the talismanic practices he recommends, the musical selections he prescribes—all operate within a framework of natural causation, not supernatural intervention.

item.title: Plotinus (204–270): Neoplatonism, Emanation, and the Divine Hierarchy
item.description:
Life and Philosophical Mission

Plotinus (204–270) was the founder of Neoplatonism and one of the most influential philosophers in Western intellectual history. Born in Lycopolis, Egypt, he studied philosophy in Alexandria before settling in Rome around 244, where he taught for thirty years and gathered a devoted circle of students.

Though Plotinus himself left no writings, his student Porphyry edited and published his writings after his death in six groups of nine treatises each—the Enneads (meaning “nines”). These writings became the definitive exposition of Neoplatonic philosophy and profoundly shaped medieval, Islamic, and Renaissance thought.

item.title: Porphyry (234–305): Neoplatonic Transmission, Theurgy, and Theological Integration
item.description:
Life and Philosophical Legacy

Porphyry (234–305), a student of Plotinus and one of antiquity’s most prolific philosophers, served as the crucial transmitter and interpreter of Neoplatonic thought. Born in Tyre, he studied under Longinus before coming to Rome to study with Plotinus around 262. After Plotinus’s death, Porphyry left Rome for Sicily, where he wrote extensively and died.

Porphyry was a systematic philosopher who organized and developed Plotinus’s teachings, created the classification of philosophical schools that shaped medieval thought, and engaged deeply with questions of theology, epistemology, and ritual practice. His Launching Points to the Realm of Mind and his Letter to Anebo—questions about theurgy addressed to the Egyptian priest—shaped how subsequent philosophers understood the relationship between philosophy, mysticism, and ritual operation.
